data.claim: Four events (ask.requested/answered/withdrawn/expired) folded into State.asks reproduce identical pending/answered state on replay of any prefix, and answer() refuses every non-person, non-credential actor
data.falsifier: a randomized event sequence whose replayed status differs from the live status, or an MCP-sourced/agent-marked actor that records an answer
data.mechanism: fold is a pure function of events; status derives from expires_at vs a passed-in now; answer gates on actors.resolve_actor source and capability
data.probe: grep existing approval.granted fold + actors.py; will be pinned by hypothesis-style property test
data.question: Can one local engine own request/answer/expiry/digest/code as events whose fold restores pending/answered state on replay, with a person-only answer path?

chunk_findings.detail: The fold converts the two boolean fields with `bool(...)`: `"bot_answerable": bool(d.get("bot_answerable"))` and `human=bool(d.get("human"))`. For real bools this is fine, but this engine is explicitly driven from CLI (`ddflow inbox`) and MCP, where flags arrive as strings, and Python's `bool()` on any non-empty string is `True`. Concretely: an answer posted with `--human false` (or an MCP payload `{"human": "false"}`) yields `bool("false") == True`, so the row records `human=True` for an answer a bot gave — the very distinction the field exists to preserve — and the same happens for `bot_answerable`/`--bot-answerable false`, turning a person-only ask into a bot-answerable one. Everything else in these handlers is defensively normalized (`str(d.get("type", "approval"))`, `list(d.get("options") or [])`), so the raw `bool()` coercion is out of step and silently flips the value instead of rejecting a non-bool.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/asks.py:48 (h_requested) and :69 (h_answered)

chunk_findings.detail: The question-text guard is dead code, so the documented rule "a question needs its text" is never enforced. `subject` is validated non-empty at line 95, so `not (text or subject)` at line 101 is always `False`; the `elif` can never fire. Demonstrated input: `request(log, cfg, subject="Which region?", kind=QUESTION, text="")` returns a `Requested` and writes an `ask.requested` event with `"text": ""` instead of raising `AskRefused`. That empty question then shows up in `pending()` / the `ddflow inbox`, and the text check the docstring promises ("a question needs its text") is missing (the intended guard was presumably `elif not text:`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ask/engine.py:101 (request)

chunk_findings.detail: `withdraw` performs no authorization at all, contradicting its own docstring ("The asker takes an ask back"). It accepts a bare `actor_id: str` and only checks that the ask exists and `row["state"] == PENDING` (line 225); it never checks that `actor_id` is the original asker, nor that the caller holds any capability, nor even `actor.source` — although `answer` deliberately proves the actor is a person before acting. Demonstrated input: an agent (or any other caller) runs `withdraw(log, "Q<id>", actor_id="someone-else")` on a pending approval/waiver and it is cancelled and stamped as withdrawn. Compounding this, `request` takes an `actor` argument but never records the requester in the event data (lines 112-124), so the asker identity is not recoverable even if `withdraw` wanted to check it. A related inconsistency: because the guard reads the folded `row["state"]` rather than `status(row)`, an ask that has actually lapsed (`status` reports `EXPIRED`) but has not yet been swept still has `state == PENDING` and can be "withdrawn", with the misleading error text "is not pending" never applied.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ask/engine.py:222 (withdraw)

chunk_findings.detail: The inner loop's ternary only distinguishes "path is a directory" from "path is a file"; it has no branch for "path does not exist". When a name in `("surfaces/mcp.py", "surfaces/tools", "api")` is absent, `(ROOT / "ddflow" / sub).is_dir()` is `False`, so the iterable becomes `[ROOT / "ddflow" / sub]` and the body calls `p.read_text(...)` on a non-existent path, raising `FileNotFoundError` instead of the test passing. Concretely, in a checkout whose only agent-facing surface is `ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py` (no `ddflow/api/` package and no `ddflow/surfaces/tools/` directory), `pytest tests/test_ask_engine.py::test_no_mcp_or_api_module_can_record_an_answer` errors out before asserting anything about the invariant it is supposed to guard. The same happens if MCP is packaged as `ddflow/surfaces/mcp/__init__.py` rather than a top-level `mcp.py`. The `is_dir()` guard signals the author already expected these paths to be optional, but the else-branch assumes every non-directory is a readable file; it needs to skip/`continue` when `p.exists()` is false (e.g. `Path.rglob` only for dirs, and `[p]` only when `p.is_file()`).

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier finding on these two lines was that the fold used `bool(...)` on transport-supplied strings, so `--human false` / `{"human": "false"}` recorded `human=True`. The change replaces that with an identity test (`human=d.get("human") is True`, `bot_answerable=d.get("bot_answerable") is True`), which fixes only the false-string direction and inverts the failure for the true-string direction. Given the same transport assumption the earlier finding was confirmed on — the engine is driven from `ddflow inbox` (CLI flags) and the MCP action, where a boolean arrives as a string — a genuine person answer posted as `--human true` (or MCP `{"human": "true"}`) now evaluates `"true" is True` → `False`, and the folded row records `human=False` for an outcome the module docstring describes as "an outcome a PERSON gave". Any consumer of the folded row that distinguishes human answers (audit, person-approval counts, gate/waiver promotion) sees a human answer as non-human, and with the CLI path the field can never be `True` at all because no string normalizes to the `True` singleton. The fix therefore does not answer the original finding: it needs to coerce at the boundary (e.g. accept `True`/`"true"`/`"1"` and reject `False`/`"false"`/`"0"`) rather than test identity, for both `human` and `bot_answerable`; a regression test covering only `false` would pass while leaving this case broken.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/asks.py:69 (h_answered) / :48 (h_requested)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new authorization in `withdraw` is unusable for the asker it names, because `request` never records who asked. The `ask.requested` payload built in `request` (the `data` dict with `id`, `type`, `subject`, `text`, `digest`, `options`, `expires_at`, `bot_answerable`, and optionally `code_hash`) carries no actor, and `log.append("ask.requested", ask_id, data)` is called with three positional arguments, so the event has no way to convey the asker. Every other event in this same module puts the actor in `data["by"]` — `answer` writes `"by": actor.id`, and `withdraw` itself writes `"by": actor.id` — and `verdict` reads the folded `last["answered_by"]`, which shows the fold derives the `*_by` row field from that `"by"` key. There is therefore no source at all for `row["requested_by"]`: the fold must either default it to `""` (in which case the first half of the condition is always true) or omit it (in which case the lookup raises `KeyError` instead of `AskRefused`).

Concretely, with the string-default branch: `r = request(log, cfg, subject="Which region?", kind=QUESTION, text="...")` followed by `withdraw(log, r.id, actor=the_same_person)` raises `AskRefused("only  or an approver may withdraw Q…")` — note the empty id in the message — so the documented "the asker takes an ask back" path is dead and withdrawal becomes approver-only. Prior finding 3's fix is therefore only half an answer: it added the `requested_by` comparison but not the write that would ever populate `requested_by`. The remedy is for `request` to record the asker (`"by": actor.id if actor else ""`, and require an actor at the ask sites) so `withdraw`'s asker branch can actually match.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ask/engine.py — `withdraw` (the `actor.id != row["requested_by"]` check) / `request` (the `ask.requested` payload)

chunk_findings.detail: This is prior finding #4, and the diff does not answer it: the triage says it was "fixed with a regression test", but the code is unchanged. The loop still selects its iterable with `target.rglob("*.py") if target.is_dir() else [target]`, which has no "path does not exist" branch. When any name in `("surfaces/mcp.py", "surfaces/tools", "api")` is absent, `(ROOT / "ddflow" / sub).is_dir()` is `False`, so the iterable becomes the single element `[ROOT / "ddflow" / sub]`, and `p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` is called on a non-existent path, raising `FileNotFoundError` instead of the test passing (or asserting). Concretely, in a checkout where `ddflow/api` does not exist, the very purpose of the test — proving no agent-facing module imports/records `ask.answered` — is defeated by an error rather than a clean assertion, and the test fails for an unrelated reason. A guard such as `if not target.exists(): continue` (treating an absent surface as vacuously clean) is required; it is not present.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix for the earlier boolean-coercion finding replaced `bool(...)` with an identity test against `True`. That silences the `"false"` case the earlier reviewer demonstrated, but it does not answer the finding for the other direction, and the earlier triage accepted the premise that drives it: the fold is fed from CLI/MCP flags, i.e. the values can arrive as strings. With `is True`, *any* string is now `False`, including the affirmative ones. Concretely: an answer posted with `--human true` (or an MCP payload `{"human": "true"}`, or `{"human": 1}`) folds to `human=False`, and a request with `bot_answerable = "true"` folds to `bot_answerable=False`; the row no longer records what the caller actually said. The correct handling of the string-flag input class is a coercion that maps `"true"/"1"` → `True` *and* `"false"/"0"` → `False` (or a transport-side conversion before the event is written), not an identity test that happens to make the negative case work by collapsing every non-bool to `False`. Note the asymmetry this creates with `h_requested`, which pre-seeds `"human": False`: there is now no input path by which a string flag can ever produce `human=True` in the fold.

chunk_findings.detail: `request()` writes the `ask.requested` event with a payload that contains no identity of the asker — `data` is only `id/type/subject/text/digest/options/expires_at/bot_answerable` — even though `request()` already receives an `actor` argument. Contrast this with the two other writers of ask events: `answer()` puts `"by": actor.id` into its payload, and `withdraw()` puts `"by": actor.id` into its payload. `withdraw()` then authorizes with `if actor.id != row["requested_by"] and not actor.can(CAP_APPROVE)`. Since the only code path in this module that appends `ask.requested` (this `request()`) records nothing the fold can turn into `requested_by`, on any ask created through this engine that key is either absent (the fold has no source for it, and `withdraw` raises `KeyError`, not `AskRefused`, out of the transaction) or defaults to `""` (and then `actor.id != ""` is always true, so the person who asked can never take their own ask back — only a holder of `approve` can), contradicting withdraw's own docstring "The asker (or an approver) takes a still-open ask back." Demonstrated: `r = request(log, cfg, subject="ship it", kind=APPROVAL, digest="abc", actor=alice)`; `withdraw(log, r.id, actor=alice)` cannot succeed for `alice`. Note this is a new defect introduced by the fix for the earlier finding #3: the actor was available and simply not recorded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ask/engine.py:request (`data` dict) and withdraw

chunk_findings.detail: The write path of the confirmed earlier finding #1 (a flag arriving as a string from CLI/MCP is coerced by `bool()`, where `bool("false") == True`) is still open on the request side. The handler-side normalization that fixed #1 operates on the folded value, which cannot recover the original string once `request()` has already stored a real bool: `request(log, cfg, subject="ship it", kind=APPROVAL, content="x", bot_answerable="false", actor=approver)` stores `bot_answerable=True`, so the ask is recorded as bot-answerable (and later `verdict` accepts `last["bot_answerable"]` as a substitute for a person's answer) although the caller passed `false`. Because the engine is documented as being driven from `ddflow inbox`/MCP where flags arrive as strings, this is the same silent coercion finding #1 was confirmed for, just on the append side that the fix does not reach.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ask/engine.py:request (`"bot_answerable": bool(bot_answerable)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
This is the previously-reported finding #4, and the triage's claim that it was "fixed with a regression test in tests/test_ask_engine.py" does not match the code shown: the construct is unchanged. In `test_no_mcp_or_api_module_can_record_an_answer` (lines 118-121):

```python
for sub in ("surfaces/mcp.py", "surfaces/tools", "api"):
    target = ROOT / "ddflow" / sub
    for p in target.rglob("*.py") if target.is_dir() else [target]:
        assert "services.ask" not in p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").replace("services import ask", "services.ask"), p
```

The ternary only distinguishes `target` is a directory from `target` is a file; it has no "target does not exist" branch. When a name is absent, `target.is_dir()` is `False`, so the iterable collapses to `[target]` and `p.read_text(...)` is called on a non-existent path, raising `FileNotFoundError`. Given a checkout whose agent-facing surface is `ddflow/surfaces/` but which has no `ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py`, no `ddflow/surfaces/tools/` directory and no `ddflow/api/` directory, the test errors instead of passing (a missing surface is exactly what this structural test should tolerate, not crash on). The fix should guard with `if target.exists()` before reading, e.g. skip when neither file nor directory exists.

chunk_findings.detail:
`request` never records who asked. The event payload it appends (`log.append("ask.requested", ask_id, data)`) contains only `id`, `type`, `subject`, `text`, `digest`, `options`, `expires_at`, `bot_answerable` (plus `code_hash`), even though `request` takes an `actor` argument — that argument is used solely for the `bot_answerable` capability check and is then dropped. Compare `answer`, which explicitly writes `"by": actor.id` into its event, showing the log does not attach an actor on its own. `withdraw` then relies on this never-written field:

```python
if actor.id != row["requested_by"] and not actor.can(CAP_APPROVE):
    raise AskRefused(f"only {row['requested_by']} or an approver may withdraw {ask_id}")
```

Scenario: alice (a person at her terminal, no `approve` capability) calls `request(..., actor=alice)` and gets back `Q...`; the folded row has no requester identity (absent, or a default such as `None`/`""`, depending on the fold). When she calls `withdraw(log, "Q...", actor=alice)`, `actor.id != row["requested_by"]` is true (or the lookup raises `KeyError`), and since she has no `approve` capability she is refused with "only ... may withdraw". So the asker — whom the function's own docstring says may take the ask back — can never withdraw her own ask; only approvers can, and stale asks linger until expiry. The engine must write the requester's id into the `ask.requested` payload (e.g. `"by": actor.id`) for the ownership check to be meaningful.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ask/engine.py `request` / `withdraw`

chunk_findings.detail: `live = asks_of(_state(log))` folds `log.read_all()`, and `replayed = asks_of(fold(list(events), strict=False))` folds `events = log.read_all()` — the same events from the same log. Since `fold` is deterministic, `assert replayed == live` (and the `E.status` comparison beneath it) is true by construction and can never detect a broken replay/restore path, so the test provides false confidence in the replay requirement it names.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix (append the read events into a *fresh* `EventLog` and compare `asks_of(fold(...))` against `asks_of(fold(...))`) does not remove the by-construction equality it was supposed to remove. `events = log.read_all()` is copied into `other` with `other.append(ev.kind, ev.subject, dict(ev.data))`, and `fold` is a pure, deterministic function of that event data, so `live` and `replayed` are two folds of the same event stream — the extra log only round-trips bytes and can never disagree. Concretely, if `fold` (the replay/restore core) is broken — e.g. it ignores `ask.withdrawn` events, or treats a `denied` outcome as `pending` — both `project(replayed)` and `project(live)` change together and the assertion `assert project(replayed) == project(live)` still passes; likewise the `E.status` comparison beneath it. The test therefore still provides false confidence in the replay requirement it names; a real check would compare the folded projection against a state derived independently from the operations performed in the loop (which asks were approved/denied/withdrawn vs. skipped), or invoke the actual restore entry point rather than re-folding. The comment "new ids and times" is also not true: `ev.data` carries the ask `id` (the engine stores it in the event), so `replayed` is keyed by the same ids as `live` and key equality is guaranteed. (Not re-reporting prior finding #1: the withdraw-by-asker path in this diff is consistent with the author's probe.)

chunk_findings.detail: The fix (append the read events into a *fresh* `EventLog` and compare `asks_of(fold(...))` against `asks_of(fold(...))`) does not remove the by-construction equality it was supposed to remove. `events = log.read_all()` is copied into `other` with `other.append(ev.kind, ev.subject, dict(ev.data))`, and `fold` is a pure, deterministic function of that event data, so `live` and `replayed` are two folds of the same event stream — the extra log only round-trips bytes and can never disagree. Concretely, if `fold` (the replay/restore core) is broken — e.g. it ignores `ask.withdrawn` events, or treats a `denied` outcome as `pending` — both `project(replayed)` and `project(live)` change together and the assertion `assert project(replayed) == project(live)` still passes; likewise the `E.status` comparison beneath it. The test therefore still provides false confidence in the replay requirement it names; a real check would compare the folded projection against a state derived independently from the operations performed in the loop (which asks were approved/denied/withdrawn vs. skipped), or invoke the actual restore entry point rather than re-folding. The comment "new ids and times" is also not true: `ev.data` carries the ask `id` (the engine stores it in the event), so `replayed` is keyed by the same ids as `live` and key equality is guaranteed. (Not re-reporting prior finding #1: the withdraw-by-asker path in this diff is consistent with the author's probe.)
